title: What Makes a Number Perfect?
author: Dan Murphy
summary: Dan Murphy describes a classroom lesson on perfect numbers that is deliberately not on any test, using it to recover the Greek idea of arithmetike, the study of what numbers are apart from how we calculate with them. He guides students through Euclid's definitions of a part and a perfect number, drawing on Nicomachus's analogy between a perfect number and a virtuous person whose parts are balanced. Students find 6 and 28, are told of 496 and 8,128, and learn that Nicomachus guessed wrong about the digit count and final digit of the next perfect number. The lesson extends to deficient and abundant numbers, and for eighth graders to generating perfect numbers from Mersenne primes as in Euclid Book IX. High schoolers are left to prove the formula themselves in the spirit of Descartes. Every level ends with the unsolved question of whether an odd perfect number exists.
points: Perfect numbers are taught precisely because they have no practical use or test value, restoring the Greek notion of arithmetic as the study of what numbers are.
Nicomachus's analogy between balanced proper factors and a virtuous, balanced character links mathematics to moral formation.
Students experience the limits of pattern-spotting when they learn that Nicomachus guessed the next perfect number's digits wrongly.
The lesson scales from fifth grade exploration, to constructing perfect numbers from Mersenne primes, to a high school proof exercise.
Ending with the open odd perfect number problem shows young students a real unsolved puzzle they can understand.
quotes: Perfect numbers have never been on a test I’ve given. They have no practical use. That is part of why schools dropped them, and it is why I teach them.
Their relief tells you what eleven-year-olds have already learned about math: it is the stuff on the test.
A virtuous person has a balanced character: not too much or too little of what makes a person a person. Similarly, a perfect number is balanced.

Perfect numbers are rare. Deficient and abundant numbers are common. In the same way, virtuous people are rare, whereas people who have an excess or deficiency of fear or moderation or any other character trait are common.

Euclid proved that the formula always produces a perfect number, but he did not prove that every perfect number comes from it. About two thousand years later, Leonhard Euler proved that every even perfect number does.
The pattern so far suggests that there are no odd perfect numbers. But remember Nicomachus’ mistakes: a pattern doesn’t prove anything.
Write “Perfect Numbers” on the board before class and don’t explain it. When they ask, “Should we take notes?” tell them not to.
